operating_point.type: rank/percentile-based, NOT a fixed probability threshold
operating_point.rationale: Notebook 08 Section 3.3 + this notebook Section 3.2 -- a fixed probability cutoff calls a very different fraction of the list depending on the underlying regime; percentile cutoffs don't.

test_evaluation.caveat: Test positive rate (39.5%) is a crisis-period upper bound per Notebook 04, not a steady-state estimate -- see Section 3.1.

known_limitations: Not probability-calibrated; use rank-based thresholds only. TESTED post-hoc (see reports/model_improvement_experiments.json): CalibratedClassifierCV improves Brier score by ~65% (0.335 -> ~0.12) but costs 42-54% of validation PR-AUC (0.196 -> 0.09-0.11). Given the operating point below is rank-based, not a fixed probability cutoff, ranking quality is what matters operationally -- calibration is therefore deliberately NOT applied, as a tested decision rather than an unexamined gap.
False negative rate is uneven across job segments (Notebook 08).
Trained predominantly on a low-conversion (2008) regime; performance degrades on later, higher-conversion periods (Notebooks 01/04/08/09).

Real cost-per-call / profit-per-subscription figures were never supplied -- the working top-15% operating point is provisional. Placeholder figures now live in reports/business_assumptions.json, the single place to update once Finance/Marketing supply real numbers (previously these only existed as inline notebook variables).
post_hoc_improvement_attempts: Four independent attempts to beat this model on validation PR-AUC (wider HistGradientBoosting search, wider Random Forest search, RF+LogReg ensembling, hand-crafted interaction features) all underperformed the tuned Random Forest above. See reports/model_improvement_experiments.json for the full negative-result log. Treated as moderate evidence this model is near what this feature set can extract, not proof of a global optimum.

measured_temporal_decay.method: 8-block expanding-window rolling-origin backtest across the full chronological dataset; see reports/rolling_origin_backtest.json and Notebook 10.
measured_temporal_decay.headline_finding: Lift over naive at the operating point ranged 0.77x-1.25x across 7 out-of-time origins. At origin 4 specifically, lift was 0.77x -- WORSE than calling customers at random -- before recovering at later origins.
measured_temporal_decay.why_this_belongs_here_not_just_in_the_de: Previous versions of this model card only asserted that test-period metrics are an 'upper bound' due to the crisis-recovery regime shift. That is true but understates the risk: this backtest shows performance can drop below the naive baseline in some windows, not just fluctuate around a lower level. The monitoring plan's realized-performance trigger (reports/monitoring_plan.json) should treat ANY observed lift below 1.0x on live data as an immediate retrain trigger, not wait for a quarterly checkpoint.

class_balancing_strategy.used: class_weight='balanced' (Random Forest), confirmed by direct inspection of the fitted estimator, not just the tuning config.
class_balancing_strategy.benchmarked_against: SMOTE (hand-implemented, imbalanced-learn unavailable), random oversampling, random undersampling -- all to 1:1. class_weight='balanced' had the best validation PR-AUC (0.193) of all five strategies tested under otherwise-identical hyperparameters. SMOTE had the best ROC-AUC (0.624) but worse PR-AUC (0.167); PR-AUC is the correct metric for this precision-at-the-top business action, so class_weight remains the right choice. Full comparison: reports/balancing_comparison.json.

confidence_intervals.method: 2000-resample non-parametric bootstrap, stratified to discard zero-positive resamples.
confidence_intervals.test_recall_at_15pct_95ci: [0.235, 0.258] around point estimate 0.246 -- i.e. even at the upper end of the interval, at least 74% of subscribers are missed at this operating point.

causal_uplift_scope: This is a response-propensity model, not an uplift/causal model, and cannot be made into one with this data. Checked directly: every row in the dataset represents a customer who WAS called in the current campaign -- there is no untreated control group to estimate the incremental effect of calling vs. not calling. This is a structural data-collection limitation, not a modeling gap; no estimator (T-learner, causal forest, etc.) resolves it without a designed experiment (a randomized calling holdout in a future campaign). See Notebook 10 Section 5.
